Then, we use the difference between the optimized node features 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new} and the input node features 𝐗 ′ = f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) \mathbf{X}^{\prime}=f^{1}(\mathbf{X}) as the target for the next decision trees built by GBDT. If l = 1 l=1 , the difference 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ − 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}-\mathbf{X}^{\prime} exactly equals the negative gradient of the loss function w.r.t. the input features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} multiplied by the learning rate η \eta :

𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ = 𝐗 ′ − η ​ ∂ L ⁡ ( g θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ′ ) , Y ) ∂ 𝐗 ′ . \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}=\mathbf{X}^{\prime}-\eta\frac{\partial L(g_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}),Y)}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{\prime}}\,.

Intuitively, BGNN model consists of two consecutive blocks, GBDT and GNN, which are trained end-to-end, and therefore can be interpreted from two angles: GBDT as an embedding layer for GNN or GNN as a parametric loss function for GBDT. In the former case, GBDT transforms the original input features 𝐗 \mathbf{X} to new node features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} which are then passed to GNN. In the latter case, one can see BGNN as a standard gradient boosted training where GNN acts as a complex loss function that depends on the graph topology.
